lessons.title: Where Debt Comes From in India: Banks, NBFCs, Venture Debt and Corporate Bonds

children.text: Most Indian companies have exactly one debt relationship: the bank their current account sits in. When that bank says no, or says yes at a price the company does not like, the conversation usually ends. It should not. India has a wider lending market than it had ten years ago, and the right source depends on how much you need, how fast, for how long, and what you can offer as security.

body.text: There is no single market for corporate debt. There is a ladder of lenders, each with a different appetite, speed and price. Borrowing well means knowing which rung you belong on today, and which one you are trying to reach.

children.text: The Lender Map

cells: Established businesses with financials, cash flows and security
Borrowers the banks find too small, too new or too complex
Typically 2 to 6 percentage points above banks
Loss-making startups that have raised institutional equity
Depends almost entirely on the credit rating
Strong companies borrowing for under a year
MSME suppliers with invoices on large buyers
Priced off the buyer's credit, not the seller's
Companies with foreign currency earnings or strong parentage
Often free, sometimes priced into the invoice

body.text: The cheapest debt in most Indian companies is the one nobody negotiates: credit from suppliers. Thirty extra days from a vendor funds working capital at no stated interest. Before arranging a loan for a short cash gap, check whether the gap can be closed on the purchase side instead.

children.text: Banks: Cheapest, Slowest, Most Conditions

Banks remain the backbone of Indian corporate borrowing. They offer the lowest rates because their own cost of funds is low, and they ask the most questions for the same reason. A typical corporate relationship has two halves.

body.caption: The two halves of a bank relationship

cells: Long-lived assets: plant, machinery, buildings, expansion
Day-to-day working capital: stock and receivables
Continuously, as money moves in and out of the account
A fixed short-term chunk of working capital
Bullet repayment, typically within a year
Invoices already raised but not yet paid
By the customer, when they pay
Letter of credit and bank guarantee
Nothing, unless invoked, when it becomes a loan

children.text: A
cash credit
limit is not a fixed loan. The bank sanctions a ceiling, but what you can actually draw on any given day is the
drawing power

, recalculated from your stock and receivables statements, less creditors, after applying a margin. Companies are regularly surprised when a ₹2 crore limit yields far less than ₹2 crore of usable cash because inventory has fallen.

markDefs.definition: A running working capital account with a sanctioned limit. The borrower draws and repays as needed, and interest is charged only on the amount actually used.
The amount a borrower may actually draw against a working capital limit at a point in time, calculated from the value of stock and receivables less creditors, after a margin.

body.text: Working capital limits are usually renewable annually, which means the bank re-examines your business every year and can reduce the limit. A facility you have treated as permanent can shrink exactly when trading conditions are hardest. Never plan a business on the assumption that a renewable limit will always be renewed at the same size.

body.title: Why MSMEs often get a better hearing than they expect

children.text: The RBI requires banks to lend a defined proportion of their credit to priority sectors, and micro, small and medium enterprises are one of those sectors. That creates real institutional pressure to lend to smaller businesses, which is why bank staff will sometimes work harder on an MSME file than its size alone would justify.

Alongside this sit the government-backed routes covered in Chapter 1, principally CGTMSE guarantees that let a bank lend without collateral, and Mudra loans for micro enterprises. The practical implication: a small business that has been refused once should ask specifically whether the proposal was considered under a guarantee scheme, because the answer is often no.
Registration on the Udyam portal is what formally establishes MSME status, and lenders will ask for it.
NBFCs: Faster, Costlier, More Flexible

Non-banking financial companies lend without holding a banking licence. They cannot take deposits the way banks do, so their own funding is more expensive, and that shows up in their lending rates. What they sell is not price. It is speed, flexibility and a willingness to look at borrowers banks reject.

columns.label: A bank is usually right when
points: The business has three years of clean audited financials
There is property or plant to offer as security
The requirement is large and can wait a few weeks
You want the cheapest long-term money available

columns.label: An NBFC is often the answer when
points: The business is young, or the financials are messy for explainable reasons
The money is needed in days, not months
The loan is small enough that a bank will not prioritise it
The structure needed is unusual: lease rental discounting, loan against shares, equipment finance

children.text: Since October 2022 the RBI has regulated NBFCs under a scale-based framework, sorting them into base, middle, upper and top layers, with larger NBFCs facing bank-like supervision. For a borrower, the practical point is that not all NBFCs are alike: a large, well-rated NBFC is a stable long-term lender, while a small one may itself face funding stress and withdraw exactly when you need a renewal.

body.title: Which lender fits?
body.question: A three-year-old Indore distribution business needs ₹60 lakh within ten days to buy stock for the festive season. It is profitable but has only two years of filed financials, and its only property is on lease. Its bank has said a fresh assessment will take six weeks. What is the realistic route?
options: Wait six weeks for the bank
An NBFC facility or invoice-backed finance, accepting a higher rate for the speed
body.explanation: The festive window will not wait six weeks. A bond issue needs a rating and far more scale, and ECB is out of reach entirely. Paying 3 or 4 percentage points more for two or three months is a small price compared to missing the season, which is exactly the trade NBFCs sell.

children.text: Venture Debt: Borrowing Against Someone Else's Equity

Venture debt lends to loss-making, venture-backed startups. The lender is not underwriting profits, because there are none. It is underwriting the equity that has just landed in the bank account and the likelihood of the next round.
Usually raised alongside or shortly after an equity round, and sized as a fraction of it.
Priced in the mid-teens, with warrants giving the lender a small equity upside.
Tenure of about two to three years, often with a short interest-only period.
Used to extend runway, fund working capital or buy equipment without further dilution.

body.text: Venture debt is repaid from the next equity round far more often than from operating cash flow. If the funding market turns and the next round does not happen, the repayment schedule does not pause. This is how a facility taken to reduce dilution ends up forcing a down round on much worse terms.

children.text: The Bond Market: Borrowing from Investors Instead of a Bank
A larger company can skip the bank and borrow directly from investors by issuing a
non-convertible debenture
. Mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds and foreign portfolio investors buy these instruments for the yield.

markDefs.definition: A debt instrument issued by a company that pays interest and repays principal, and never converts into shares. Shortened to NCD.

body.label: The Indian corporate bond market
body.value: Roughly ₹53 to ₹58 lakh crore outstanding, with around ₹10 lakh crore raised in FY25
body.context: It has compounded at about 12% a year over the past decade and is still small relative to bank credit, which is why SEBI and the RBI keep pushing to deepen it. For issuers with a good rating, it is often cheaper than a bank loan and comes with fewer operating conditions.

children.text: Two things decide whether this route is open to you. The first is size: below roughly ₹50 crore to ₹100 crore, the cost and effort rarely justify it. The second is a
credit rating
from an agency such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings. The rating, not your relationship with a banker, sets your price.

markDefs.definition: An opinion from an agency such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings on how likely an issuer is to repay on time. It largely determines the interest rate a bond issuer pays.

body.title: Indicative borrowing cost by source (% a year)

body.caption: Two ways to issue bonds in India

cells: Faster, through an electronic bidding platform
Full offer document, SEBI process, longer timeline
The overwhelming majority of Indian corporate bond issuance
Occasional, often by NBFCs raising retail money

children.text: SEBI requires private placements of debt securities to go through an electronic book provider platform once the issue crosses a threshold, and that threshold was lowered to ₹20 crore in 2025 from ₹50 crore earlier. The purpose is price discovery: bidding happens on a platform rather than through bilateral phone calls.

body.title: The EBP threshold
body.textWithBlank: Private placements of debt securities must use SEBI's electronic bidding platform once the issue size reaches ₹___ crore.
body.explanation: The threshold was reduced from ₹50 crore to ₹20 crore in 2025, bringing many more mid-size issues onto a transparent bidding platform.

body.title: What the rating buys
body.question: Two companies issue five-year bonds on the same day. One is rated AAA and prices at about 7.5%. The other is rated A and prices at about 10%. On a ₹500 crore issue, roughly how much more does the lower-rated company pay in interest each year?
options: Nothing, because the rating only affects who can buy
body.explanation: 2.5 percentage points on ₹500 crore is ₹12.5 crore a year, or ₹62.5 crore over five years. This is why companies invest real effort in their credit rating, and why the next lesson treats ratings as part of the cost of debt rather than an administrative formality.

children.text: TReDS: The Route Most MSMEs Do Not Use

An MSME supplying a large buyer usually waits 45 to 90 days to be paid. TReDS, the Trade Receivables Discounting System, is an RBI-approved marketplace where that supplier can sell the invoice to financiers who bid to buy it. Platforms include RXIL, M1xchange and Invoicemart.
The critical feature is whose credit is being priced. In
bill discounting

through TReDS, financiers are taking the risk of the large buyer, not the small supplier. A tiny vendor supplying a blue-chip corporate can therefore raise money at a rate its own balance sheet would never command.

markDefs.definition: Selling an unpaid invoice to a financier at a discount to receive cash immediately, instead of waiting for the customer to pay.

body.caption: The cost of getting paid early instead of waiting

body.title: Price the early payment
body.prompt: An MSME discounts a ₹50 lakh invoice on TReDS at an annualised rate of 10%, 60 days before the buyer is due to pay. What does the early payment cost, in ₹? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: ₹50,00,000 times 10% times 60 divided by 365 is about ₹82,192. The supplier receives roughly ₹49.18 lakh immediately instead of ₹50 lakh two months later. Whether that is worth it depends on what the cash unlocks: if it funds the next order at a 15% margin, easily.

body.label: Receivables Exchange of India (RXIL)
body.description: One of the RBI-licensed TReDS platforms. Worth understanding how registration, buyer onboarding and bidding work before assuming your invoices cannot be financed.

children.text: External Commercial Borrowings

Indian companies can also borrow from lenders outside India, under the RBI's ECB framework. The attraction is a lower headline interest rate abroad. The catch is currency risk: if you earn in rupees and repay in dollars, a depreciating rupee raises your repayment in rupee terms, and hedging that risk costs money that often erases the saving.

body.text: The ECB framework has been revised repeatedly, most recently in 2026, changing the automatic route limits and the cost ceilings that had applied for years. Treat any summary of ECB rules, including this one, as a prompt to check the current RBI regulations rather than as the current position.

body.title: One company, four needs, four lenders
body.scenario: You are the finance manager of a Pune auto components company with ₹120 crore of revenue, profitable, with a rated balance sheet and a factory it owns. Four requirements land in the same quarter. A: ₹25 crore for a new machining line with an eight-year life. B: ₹12 crore of extra working capital because a large OEM customer has moved from 45-day to 75-day payment terms. C: ₹3 crore urgently, within a week, to secure a raw material lot at a favourable price. D: ₹60 crore in two years to refinance existing loans at a better rate.
body.prompt: Match each requirement to a source, and say why.
body.modelAnswer:
A, the machining line: a bank term loan, secured against the machine itself, with a tenure matched to the asset life of around seven to eight years. This is exactly what banks price best, and the company has the financials and security to command a good spread.

B, the stretched receivables: two options. A higher cash credit limit is the conventional answer, but the better one may be TReDS. The OEM is a large, well-rated buyer, so invoices on it can be discounted at a rate driven by the OEM's credit rather than the company's. That converts a permanent working capital problem into a per-invoice cost, and does not consume the company's own limit.

C, ₹3 crore in a week: the bank will not move that fast on a fresh proposal. Either draw on an existing sanctioned limit if there is headroom, which is the cheapest and fastest option, or use an NBFC for a short-tenor facility. Paying 12% a year on ₹3 crore costs about ₹69,000 a week, so roughly ₹2.1 lakh for three weeks, which is easily justified if the raw material discount is larger than that.

D, ₹60 crore refinancing in two years: this one has lead time, so use it. With a rating already in place, test the bond market. An NCD issue at a AAA or AA rate could price below the bank loan and come with fewer operating conditions, and the two-year runway is enough to improve the rating first. Run it as a competitive process against the existing bank, because the threat of refinancing elsewhere is itself a negotiating tool.

The pattern: match tenure to asset life, match the security to the lender who values it most, and use whoever is fastest when speed is the binding constraint.

body.title: Before choosing a lender
steps: How quickly do we actually need the money, and what does a delay cost?
What security can we offer, and which lender values it most?
Does the tenure on offer match the life of what we are funding?
Have we compared the all-in cost, including fees, not just the rate?
If we are an MSME, have we asked about CGTMSE-backed lending and TReDS?
If we have a rating, have we priced a bond issue against the bank loan?
Is this lender likely to still be there at renewal, and what happens if it is not?

cards.definition: A running working capital limit where interest is charged only on the amount drawn.
What you can actually draw against a limit, based on stock and receivables less creditors.
A non-deposit-taking lender: faster and more flexible than a bank, and more expensive.
Loans to venture-backed startups, repaid largely out of the next equity round.
Non-convertible debenture. Borrowing directly from investors, priced off a credit rating.
SEBI's electronic bidding platform, mandatory for private debt placements of ₹20 crore and above.
An RBI-approved platform for discounting MSME invoices, priced on the buyer's credit.
Borrowing from lenders outside India under the RBI framework, carrying currency risk.

points: Indian debt is a ladder: supplier credit, banks, small finance banks, NBFCs, venture debt, bonds, commercial paper, TReDS and ECB.
Banks are cheapest and slowest. NBFCs sell speed and flexibility at 2 to 6 percentage points more.
A cash credit limit is not guaranteed cash: drawing power depends on stock and receivables, and limits are re-examined annually.
Venture debt is repaid out of the next equity round more often than out of operations, which is its central risk.
Bond market access depends on size and a credit rating, and the rating alone can be worth crores a year.
TReDS lets an MSME borrow at its large buyer's credit quality rather than its own, and remains underused.
ECB looks cheap until currency risk and hedging costs are counted, and its rules change frequently.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Rates shown are indicative and vary by borrower, security and date. Market sizes and regulatory thresholds were as reported when written and change: verify current RBI and SEBI requirements before acting. Named platforms and rating agencies are examples of the Indian market, not recommendations.
